title: Pilot study for the identification of potential risk factors for perioperative myocardial injury (PMI) and proof-of-concept for an AI-based risk score
summary:
Perioperative myocardial injury (PMI) occurring during or within 3 days of an operation affects approximately 20 per cent of all surgical patients who are not undergoing primary heart surgery. This means that just under 1,400,000 patients are affected each year. It has been shown that, in around three-quarters of cases, this damage to the heart muscle is partly caused or brought about by a dysfunction of the smallest blood vessels in the heart. These smallest vessels are no longer able to dilate as required, leading to a relative undersupply of blood to the heart muscle tissue. The rates of serious complications and mortality are both 22%.
Given the frequency and significance of this myocardial damage, repeated measurements of the cardiac-specific biomarker hs-troponin T are recommended for patients with moderate to high perioperative risk. Another relevant factor in this context is heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) or diastolic dysfunction, which is not currently routinely assessed prior to surgery by means of a cardiac ultrasound, but which frequently occurs in conjunction with the described myocardial ischaemia.
Study procedure
Following approval by the Ethics Committee and the patients’ consent to participate in the study, participants will undergo a cardiac ultrasound scan prior to surgery, with the primary focus on identifying any potential diastolic dysfunction. In addition, two blood tubes (plasma, serum) will be collected, at the latest during the induction phase, for a project-specific biobank, in order to subsequently carry out further microRNA analyses for potential risk factors as well as troponin fragmentation analyses. During the induction of anaesthesia, whole blood is collected from patients both before the anaesthetic is administered and post-operatively to determine various laboratory parameters (including NT-proBNP, hs-troponin T/I, endothelial biomarkers, inflammatory markers, etc.). The necessary venous accesses are established as part of standard anaesthesiological care. These additional parameters are predominantly determined from blood samples taken independently of the study. Only the measurements of the cardiac-specific biomarker troponin T/I immediately post-operatively or at 20:00 are carried out via additional blood sampling.
Postoperatively, laboratory parameter measurements continue for three days. High-sensitivity troponin T/I is measured within the first 24 hours, immediately after surgery and, if necessary, at 20:00, to ensure the earliest possible detection of cardiac muscle damage. Thereafter, measurements are taken once daily for three days postoperatively. In the event of a significant increase in hs-troponin T/I, an ultrasound scan of the heart is performed to assess current cardiac function, particularly diastolic function. In addition, two further blood tubes (plasma, serum) are collected for the project-specific biobank. A repeat NT-proBNP measurement is also carried out.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Patients with non-cardiac surgery
Exclusion criteria:
Age <40 years
Pregnancy and breastfeeding
Operations on patients with congenital heart defects
Operations on patients with long-term corticosteroid therapy
Patients with calcium antagonists and/or nitrates in prior medication
Emergency operations
Patients with cardiac devices and post heart valve replacement
Patients with Raynaud's syndrome and/or PAD and/or vasculitis
